subLevels.german: Es waren einmal drei Bären: Vater Bär, Mutter Bär und Bärchen.

hints.hint: This is the beginning of a familiar fairytale. Use the traditional English beginning to such a story.
"-chen" is a diminutive, making a Bär a little Bär.

subLevels.reveal: The original story had three male bears: der große Bär, der mittlere Bär und der kleine Bär, by size.

hints.hint: Ein Nilpferd ist auch ein Tier.
Think of how you would answer the traditional first question in Twenty Questions if the target was a Bär.

subLevels.reveal: The English word "deer" used to mean all animals, just like Tier in German, but its scope shrank to just one type of animal.

subLevels.german: Im Tiergarten Schönbrunn, dem ältesten Zoo der Welt, kann man Bären finden.
subLevels.instruction: Translate, keeping the same clause order.

hints.hint: English uses a slightly different preposition for the first word.
If Tier ~ "deer", then ält ~ what English adjective?
German Mann means "man" but German man, which derives from it, is an impersonal pronoun.

subLevels.reveal: German used to use Tiergarten for zoos in general when they grew out of private hunting grounds, but now the word "Zoo" is more widely used. Our word "kindergarten" was also borrowed from German, with Kind meaning a child. Not to imply that kindergartens were conceived of as zoos for children!

subLevels.instruction: Answer the question by filling in the blanks (-1 pt per invalid move)
subLevels.german: Wo kann man in Wien Bären finden?

hints.hint: "Wo" is a question word meaning "where".
"Wien" is a major Austrian city.

subLevels.reveal: Notice here that an entire prepositional phrase can fit into the first slot! Even the appositive phrase dem ältesten Zoo der Welt could fit in there with it. So even though we call it "verb-second", the conjugated verb may actually sit very far away from the beginning of a sentence.

subLevels.german: Aber diese drei Bären leben in einem kleinen Haus im Wald.

hints.hint: It may be tempting to think that Wald ~ "wild", but they are unrelated. Think 🌲🌲 instead.

subLevels.reveal: Wald only persists in English in the archaic word "weald" and place names like the Cotswolds.

subLevels.german: „Ich bin so hungrig!“ denkt Goldlöckchen. „Ich möchte den Bärenbrei essen!“

hints.hint: If Donner ~ "thunder", then denk(t) ~ ?
We've seen möchte before in the lament Ich möchte nicht arbeiten!

subLevels.reveal: Notice how "bears" and "porridge" fused together to form a single word Bärenbrei? German compounds productively, but we'll see its limits in a bit...

subLevels.german: Sie klopft an die Tür des Bärenhauses.

hints.hint: If Tier ~ "deer", then Tür ~ ? The vowel does change a bit!
The verb klopfen is onomatopoeic. Try saying "klop klop" to yourself.

subLevels.reveal: Nice job! It looks very much like the bears own multiple houses, but in this economy?! Bärenhauses is still singular, it's just in the genitive case just like der Welt ("of the world"), which we saw in level 3.

subLevels.german: Vater Bärs Brei war zu heiß, Mutter Bärs Brei war zu kalt, aber Bärchens Brei war genau richtig.

hints.hint: This is our first time seeing ß, it represents "ss".
war is the past tense of ist.
You'll hear genau ("exactly" is its more usual translation) a lot in conversational German to express agreement.

subLevels.reveal: We have the more English-like possessive "Vater Bärs Brei" here rather than something like Vaterbärenbrei. German uses s rather than compounding when indicating specific ownership.

subLevels.english: Goldilocks falls asleep in Baby Bear's bed.
subLevels.reveal: Surprise! The verb einschlafen "to fall asleep" is our first separable verb. ein indicates "entering a state of" and schlafen means "sleep" (the English and German are cognates!). When a separable verb moves to V2 position, it leaves its prefix stranded in the final position of the clause. Mark Twain skewered this hilariously in his famous essay on German.

subLevels.german: „Jemand hat von meinem Brei gegessen ... und hat ihn aufgegessen!“

hints.hint: ihn is a pronoun replacing a noun seen earlier in the sentence.
getrunken : trinken :: ge(g)essen : ?. (We've already seen this verb in this level!)
auf- is another separable prefix. It often intensifies a verb to mean something has happened completely.
Recall that noble names like "von Clausewitz" indicate that the person's family is ___ a place called Clausewitz.

subLevels.reveal: aufessen is another separable verb ("to eat up/completely"). Notice how its past participle is constructed: auf- (separable prefix) + ge- (past participle marker) + (g)essen (past participle of essen). The ge- slips between the prefix and the verb stem, a quirk specific to separable verbs. The extra g- is just because essen is irregular.

subLevels.german: Goldlöckchen wacht auf und rennt weg, so schnell sie kann!

hints.hint: sag ~ "say" so weg ~ ? Add an "a" to the beginning to get the English equivalent.
If Buch ~ "book" then wach(t) ~ ?
schnell is commonly heard in Zweiter Weltkrieg movies being shouted at POWs or underlings to hurry up.

subLevels.reveal: More separable verbs! Most such verbs correspond to phrasal verbs in English, as with aufwachen "wake up" and wegrennen "run away". But sometimes we have "fall asleep" rather than "sleep into", as with einschlafen earlier. I hope this level wasn't zu schwer oder zu leicht, aber genau richtig!
